opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a few things have come together at the same time. First, the research has matured. For a long time diffusion models dominated images, video, and audio. Language was the holdout, because text is discrete and the continuous-noise framework didn't map onto it cleanly. Over the last few years, my group and others worked out better ways to do diffusion over discrete tokens. Score entropy and masked or discrete diffusion objectives are examples. We started seeing diffusion language models that could match autoregressive models of similar size on quality. That was the turning point. Once quality is competitive, the question becomes what else you get, and with diffusion what you get is a lot.

The big one is speed and efficiency. An autoregressive model generates one token at a time, left to right. That's fundamentally sequential, and on modern GPUs it means you're often memory-bandwidth bound and not using the hardware well. A diffusion model starts with a rough draft of the whole output and refines many tokens in parallel over a number of steps. So you can produce text several times faster at the same quality, and serve it more cheaply. That really matters right now, because inference cost and latency have become the bottleneck for deploying these systems, especially for agentic workflows. There, a model might make dozens of calls before it returns an answer to a user.

There are also some nice qualitative advantages. Because the model isn't committed to whatever it wrote three tokens ago, it can go back and fix mistakes during refinement. That helps with things like code, where global consistency matters, and with editing or infilling tasks that are awkward for left-to-right generation. It also gives you a natural knob to trade compute for quality: you can run more or fewer denoising steps.

So it's the combination. The modeling ideas are finally mature enough to be competitive. The demand for faster, cheaper inference has never been higher. And the hardware favors parallel computation. That made it feel like the right moment to take this out of the lab and actually put it in people's hands.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are really a couple of things coming together at once. The first is just the science. Diffusion models completely took over images, video, audio — basically every continuous modality — and for a long time the conventional wisdom was that they just don't work for text, because text is discrete and you can't add Gaussian noise to a token. We spent years in my lab at Stanford working on that problem, on how to do diffusion over discrete data, and at some point the quality gap just closed. Our models became competitive with autoregressive models of the same size, and once that happened the question changed from "can this work?" to "why aren't we using this?"

And the reason you'd want to use it comes down to the fundamental limitation of autoregressive generation. Every frontier LLM today produces text one token at a time, left to right. That's a sequential bottleneck that no amount of hardware fixes — you can't parallelize it, so you're paying for a full forward pass per token, and you're stuck with latency that scales linearly with the length of the output. Diffusion doesn't have that constraint. You start from noise and refine the whole sequence in parallel, so you can generate many tokens per step. In practice we're seeing something like five to ten times the throughput on the same GPUs, and that's not an incremental optimization, that's a structural change.

The second thing is the market. Two years ago the conversation was mostly about capability — can the model do the task at all. Now people are actually deploying these things at scale, and the costs are enormous. Inference is the dominant line item. And a lot of the most interesting applications — agents, coding assistants, anything with a tight interactive loop — are really latency bound. If an agent has to make twenty model calls to complete a task, the speed of each call determines whether the product is usable. So suddenly speed and cost aren't nice-to-haves, they're the thing that decides whether a use case is viable.

And then the third piece is that the surrounding infrastructure is finally mature enough. The tooling, the serving stacks, the evaluation methods — a lot of that transfers over. We don't have to rebuild the entire ecosystem; we can plug into what people are already doing.

So you put those together — the research matured, the economic pressure is real, and the infrastructure exists — and it felt like exactly the moment to go from papers to something people can actually build on. That's really the bet behind Inception.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that we’re seeing a path from an interesting research idea to something that offers a practical advantage. With autoregressive models, you generate one token at a time, and each token has to wait for the previous one. Diffusion gives you a different way to approach that computation: you can refine multiple parts of the output in parallel.

Now, that doesn’t automatically make it faster. You have to account for how many refinement steps you need and what quality you get at the end. But it gives us another dimension to optimize, especially when latency and inference cost matter.

So the reason to bring it into production now is to test that tradeoff on real workloads. Can we deliver the quality users need with a better latency or cost profile? I don’t think diffusion has to replace autoregressive models everywhere to be useful. It needs to offer a meaningful advantage for the applications where its strengths matter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re at a point where the quality is becoming competitive, and we can start to take advantage of what makes diffusion different. With an autoregressive model, you generate one token at a time, so there’s a sequential bottleneck. With diffusion, you can update many positions in parallel and refine the answer over multiple steps.

That creates an interesting opportunity: can we deliver comparable quality with lower latency or lower cost? And can we give users more control over the tradeoff between speed and how much computation the model spends refining an answer?

Of course, parallel generation doesn’t automatically make a system faster. The number of refinement steps and the efficiency of the implementation matter a lot. But the models and the infrastructure are reaching the point where we can test those advantages in real applications. That’s what makes this an exciting time to bring them into production.
